Setup Guide

This guide provides step-by-step instructions for installing and running PlaViSCA locally.

System Requirements

  • Operating System: macOS, Windows, or Linux

  • R Version: 4.3.3 (tested) (Download R)

  • RStudio: 2024.09 or later (recommended) (Download RStudio)

  • Git: 2.43 or later (Download Git)

  • RAM: 8 GB minimum (one instance of the app uses about 2 GB with the normalized data, 3 GB once the raw data are loaded)

  • CPU: 4 cores minimum

  • Disk Space: 5 GB free

Environment Snapshot (current)

The live app was run with the following versions:

  • R: 4.3.3

  • renv: 1.1.7

  • Core packages: bslib (0.9.0), conflicted (1.2.0), DT (0.34.0), dplyr (1.1.4), fontawesome (0.5.3), later (1.4.5), memoise (2.0.1), plotly (4.11.0), RColorBrewer (1.1-3), readr (2.1.6), shiny (1.12.1), shinycssloaders (1.1.0), shinyjs (2.1.1), stringr (1.6.0), tibble (3.3.1), tidyverse (2.0.0), viridis (0.6.5), writexl (1.5.4)

If you restore with renv, these exact versions will be installed automatically.

Installation Steps

PlaViSCA is compatible with macOS, Windows, and Linux operating systems. Follow the steps below to set up the application on your system.

1. Clone the Repository

git clone https://github.com/baia-ipc/PlaViSCA-app.git
cd PlaViSCA-app

This will create a directory named PlaViSCA-app containing all application files.

2. Install Dependencies

Recommended — restore exact versions with renv:

install.packages("renv")
renv::restore()

This installs the exact package versions listed above. If you prefer a minimal install without renv, use:

install.packages(c(
  "shiny", "shinyjs", "shinycssloaders", "plotly", "DT",
  "RColorBrewer", "tidyverse", "later", "memoise", "viridis",
  "readr", "tibble", "bslib", "fontawesome", "conflicted", "writexl"
))

Notes for macOS

renv installs ready-built packages where it can, and compiles the others from source. Compiling needs Apple’s command line tools:

xcode-select --install

The packages openssl, curl and xml2 link to system libraries, and two common setups make them fail to build or load:

  • conda or mamba on the PATH. Their copies of these libraries get picked up, and the installed package then fails to load with Library not loaded: @rpath/.... Run conda deactivate (repeat until no environment is active), or remove conda from the PATH in that terminal, before renv::restore().

  • Homebrew’s OpenSSL 4. The openssl package version used here builds against OpenSSL 3 (errors such as incomplete definition of type 'const ASN1_BIT_STRING'). Install OpenSSL 3 and point the build at it:

    brew install openssl@3
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$(brew --prefix openssl@3)/lib/pkgconfig"
R -e 'renv::restore()'

renv::restore() installs all packages or none: after fixing a failed package, run it again. Any R 4.3.x works; with a version other than 4.3.3, R prints harmless warnings that packages were built under another version.

3. Prepare the Data

PlaViSCA reads its data from the directory named by the PLAVISCA_DATA_DIR environment variable (default: data/ inside the app directory). This directory must contain:

File

Description

cleaned_dataset.rds

Per-cell metadata and embeddings, per-study PCA and variable-gene tables

normalized_expression.rds

Log-normalised expression: a sparse matrix (Matrix::dgCMatrix), cells x genes, rows named by cell barcode in the order of the metadata, columns by gene ID

raw_expression.rds

Raw counts, same layout

gene_annotation.rds

P. vivax P01 gene identifiers, names and descriptions

data_source.csv

Publication table for the Data Sources tab

These files are written by the PlaViSCA preprocessing pipeline into the results/app_data/ directory of a pipeline run. Point the app at them, for example:

export PLAVISCA_DATA_DIR=/path/to/run/results/app_data

At startup the app checks that the data match its configuration (studies, columns, life-cycle stages). If they do not, it stops with a message listing what is wrong.

4. Run the Application

Option A: Using the helper script (Linux/macOS — Recommended)

A bash script is provided to simplify running the app, especially on servers.

chmod +x run_app.sh
./run_app.sh

To expose the app on a specific host and port:

./run_app.sh --host 0.0.0.0 --port 3838

Available options:

Flag

Description

Default

-h, --host

Host IP address

0.0.0.0

-p, --port

Port number

3838

-b, --browser

Auto-open browser on launch

disabled

--help

Show usage information

—

Then open a browser and go to: http://localhost:3838 (or replace localhost with your server IP).

Option B: Using RStudio (Desktop)

  1. Open RStudio and set the working directory to the PlaViSCA-app project folder.

  2. Open app.R in the editor.

  3. Click the Run App button in the top-right corner of the editor pane.

The app will launch in your default web browser.

Option C: From the terminal (R command)

R -e "shiny::runApp('.', launch.browser = TRUE)"

For a server without a display:

R -e "shiny::runApp('.', host='0.0.0.0', port=3838, launch.browser=FALSE)"

Then open http://<server-ip>:3838 in a browser. Find your server IP with:

hostname -I

Serving Several Users

./run_app.sh is enough for one person, or for a few colleagues who take turns. For a public server, read on.

Why one R process is a bottleneck

A Shiny app runs in a single R process, and R does one thing at a time. All browsers connected to that process share it: while it draws a plot for one user, every other user waits, and the whole process holds one copy of the data for everybody. The remedy is to run several copies of the app (instances), each in its own R process, and to spread the users over them.

Several instances behind nginx

Start one instance per port. Each one loads its own copy of the data, which takes 2 to 3 GB of memory:

export PLAVISCA_DATA_DIR=/path/to/app_data
./run_app.sh --host 127.0.0.1 --port 3838 &
./run_app.sh --host 127.0.0.1 --port 3839 &
./run_app.sh --host 127.0.0.1 --port 3840 &
./run_app.sh --host 127.0.0.1 --port 3841 &

On a Linux server, let systemd start them at boot and restart them if they stop. The repository provides a template unit, a service definition in which %i stands for the instance name, here the port (deploy/systemd/plavisca@.service):

[Unit]
Description=PlaViSCA Shiny app on port %i
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=plavisca
WorkingDirectory=/path/to/PlaViSCA-app
Environment=PLAVISCA_DATA_DIR=/path/to/app_data
ExecStart=/path/to/PlaViSCA-app/run_app.sh --host 127.0.0.1 --port %i
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=10
TimeoutStartSec=300

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

WorkingDirectory must be the app directory: R reads the .Rprofile there, which activates the renv library with the right package versions. Install and start four instances with:

sudo cp deploy/systemd/plavisca@.service /etc/systemd/system/
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now plavisca@3838 plavisca@3839 plavisca@3840 plavisca@3841
journalctl -u plavisca@3838 -f     # follow the log of one instance

Then put nginx in front as a reverse proxy: a web server that receives the users on one address and forwards each of them to one of the instances. Two things matter for Shiny:

  • Sticky sessions. A Shiny session lives in one R process, so a browser must keep talking to the instance it started on. ip_hash sends each client address always to the same instance.

  • Websocket upgrade. Shiny keeps one open connection (a websocket) per session, and the proxy must pass the Upgrade headers through.

A complete minimal server block (deploy/nginx/plavisca.conf):

upstream plavisca {
    ip_hash;
    server 127.0.0.1:3838;
    server 127.0.0.1:3839;
    server 127.0.0.1:3840;
    server 127.0.0.1:3841;
}

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name plavisca.example.org;

    gzip on;
    gzip_types text/plain text/css application/javascript application/json
               image/svg+xml;
    gzip_min_length 1024;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://plavisca;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_read_timeout 3600s;
        proxy_send_timeout 3600s;
        proxy_buffering off;
    }
}

sudo cp deploy/nginx/plavisca.conf /etc/nginx/sites-available/plavisca
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/plavisca /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx

gzip compresses the page, scripts and styles sent over plain HTTP. The plots travel over the websocket, and websocket messages are not compressed by the proxy. For HTTPS, add a certificate (for example with certbot) to the same server block.

Alternatives

  • ShinyProxy (open source) starts one Docker container, with its own R process, per user. The strongest isolation, at the cost of one data copy per user and a container start before the first page.

  • Posit Connect and Shiny Server Pro (commercial) run several R processes per app and balance the users over them, with authentication built in.

  • Shiny Server open source runs one R process per app, with no load balancing: all users of the app share that process, as with ./run_app.sh. Simple to set up, fine for a small group.

Sizing

  • Memory: 2 to 3 GB per instance (each holds its own copy of the data: about 2 GB with the normalized data, 3 GB once the raw data are loaded), plus what the system needs. Check the instances with free -h once they are started.

  • CPU: one core per instance plus one for the proxy and the system, so four instances need five cores.

  • Users per instance: a handful; users are only served in turn while a plot is being drawn, so more instances mean shorter waits.

Locale

Shiny Server, and systemd by default, run R in the C locale (plain ASCII, no language settings). The app is written for that: its sources are ASCII and it reads and writes its files as UTF-8, so no LANG or LC_ALL setting is needed.

Troubleshooting

Problem

Solution

Browser error on launch ('browser' must be a non-empty character string)

R is trying to open a browser in a headless environment. Use ./run_app.sh (browser disabled by default) or add launch.browser = FALSE to your runApp() call.

renv::restore() fails

Run R -e "renv::status()" to identify missing packages. On Linux, you may need system libraries: sudo apt-get install libcurl4-openssl-dev libssl-dev libxml2-dev. On macOS, see Notes for macOS in Step 2.

App stops at startup with “data file(s) are missing”

Set PLAVISCA_DATA_DIR to a directory containing the five files listed in Step 3.

App stops at startup with “data check(s) failed”

The data do not match config/data_columns.yml (e.g. a different number of cells or studies). Use the data written by the matching version of the preprocessing pipeline, or update config/data_columns.yml (see the developer guide, docs/developer.md).

App is slow or crashes

Check the memory (see the system requirements) and close other applications. Starting the app takes about 20 s (reading the data and drawing the first embedding plot); the raw data are read the first time a session selects them. If several people use the app at once, run several instances behind a proxy: see Serving Several Users.

Browser display issues

Clear the browser cache or try a different browser. Ensure JavaScript is enabled.

Package not found after renv::restore()

Try renv::repair() followed by renv::restore() again.

For additional help, contact the development team or open a GitHub issue.
